hints: Think about which end of Period 3 forms strongly basic oxides that release many hydroxide ions in water.
walkthrough:
Link pH to oxide type**
A pH greater than 10 means a strongly alkaline solution, so you are looking for a strongly basic oxide. Across Period 3, basic character is strongest on the left and falls toward acidic on the right.

Pick the most basic Period 3 oxide**
$\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$ reacts to give $2\text{NaOH}$, a strong alkali: $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH}$. $\text{MgO}$ is only sparingly soluble and gives a much lower pH, so the answer is $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Recall how an acidic oxide behaves with a base, first forming phosphoric acid and then being neutralised by excess alkali.
walkthrough:
Recognise acid base chemistry**
$\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ is a strongly acidic oxide. With excess aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ it is fully neutralised to the phosphate salt plus water only, no hydrogen left in the anion.

Write the balanced equation**
With excess alkali each $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ needs $3\text{NaOH}$. Scaling to $\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10}$ gives: $$\text{P}_{4}\text{O}_{10} + 12\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 4\text{Na}_{3}\text{PO}_{4} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Work out the oxidation number of the non-oxygen element in each oxide using the rule that oxygen is -2.
walkthrough:
Calculate each oxidation number**
Let oxygen be $-2$. Then in $\text{SO}_{2}$, S is $+4$, in $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$, H is $+1$, in $\text{SO}_{3}$, S is $+6$, in $\text{SiO}_{2}$, Si is $+4$, in $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$, Na is $+1$, in $\text{MgO}$, Mg is $+2$, in $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$, Al is $+3$.

Select the highest**
The largest value is $+6$ for sulfur in $\text{SO}_{3}$, so that oxide contains the element with the highest oxidation number.

hints: Pick out the ionically bonded oxides from Table 2.1 and compare their melting points in order of cation charge.
Check whether melting point rises smoothly with cation charge, paying close attention to MgO compared with Al2O3.
walkthrough:
Identify the ionic oxides**
Think of bonding types. $\text{SO}_{2}$, $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and $\text{SO}_{3}$ are simple molecules with very low melting points. $\text{SiO}_{2}$ is giant covalent. The three with very high melting points, $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$ and $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$, are ionically bonded giant lattices.

Test the hypothesis with data**
If only cation charge mattered, melting point should rise $\text{Na}^{+}$ < $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ < $\text{Al}^{3+}$. The data show $\text{Na}_{2}\text{O}$ is $1132^{\circ}\text{C}$, $\text{MgO}$ is $2852^{\circ}\text{C}$, but $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ falls to $2072^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Conclude false**
$\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ melts lower than $\text{MgO}$ even though $\text{Al}^{3+}$ has a higher charge than $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. So charge alone does not determine melting point, other factors such as ionic radius, polarisation and lattice structure also matter.

Final answer: False.
$\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ has a lower melting point than $\text{MgO}$ but the charge on $\text{Al}^{3+}$ is greater than that on $\text{Mg}^{2+}$.

hints: Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base in terms of protons, $\text{H}^{+}$ ions.
walkthrough:
Use the Bronsted-Lowry idea**
A Bronsted-Lowry base is simply a proton acceptor. It takes $\text{H}^{+}$ from an acid.

Apply to ZnO in acid**
In $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}(\text{aq})$, the oxide ion in $\text{ZnO}$ accepts $2\text{H}^{+}$ to form water: $\text{ZnO} + 2\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Because it accepts protons, it acts as a Bronsted-Lowry base.
Final answer: $\text{ZnO}$ accepts protons / $\text{H}^{+}$ from the acid.

hints: Remember that amphoteric aluminium oxide dissolves in strong alkali to give a soluble complex anion containing Al, O and H.
walkthrough:
Spot amphoteric behaviour**
$\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ reacts with both acids and alkalis. With $\text{NaOH}(\text{aq})$ it acts as an acid and dissolves.

Name the aluminium species**
The aluminium ends up in the tetrahydroxoaluminate(III) ion, $\text{Al(OH)}_{4}^{-}$, so the compound formed is sodium aluminate: $\text{NaAl(OH)}_{4}$.

hints: Think of this as a normal base plus acid reaction where the metal forms its usual $3+$ salt with the acid anion.
walkthrough:
Treat Al2O3 as a base here**
With sulfuric acid, amphoteric $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ behaves as a base: oxide plus acid gives salt plus water.

Combine Al3+ with sulfate**
Aluminium forms $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and the acid provides $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$, so the salt is aluminium sulfate: $$\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \rightarrow \text{Al}_{2}(\text{SO}_{4})_{3} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ The aluminium-containing salt is $\text{Al}_{2}(\text{SO}_{4})_{3}$.
